name: Chervil
summary: A delicate annual or biennial culinary herb in the carrot family, with parsley-like foliage and a short harvest window before flowering. It is not parsley (Petroselinum crispum).

identity.guidance: Kew POWO accepts Anthriscus cerefolium in Apiaceae and describes it as annual or biennial. NC State Extension identifies chervil as a culinary herb and distinguishes its seed propagation from transplant-sensitive handling.

cultivation.short: Cool conditions, even moisture and partial shade in hot weather
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension describes chervil as a cool-weather herb for moist, well-drained soil in partial to full sun; RHS recommends a cool, lightly shaded position and consistently moist, not waterlogged compost, especially in hot or dry weather. These are garden/container directions, not a hydroponic recipe or indoor grow-light tier. Spacing guidance differs: Maryland Extension says thin to 3–4 inches while NC State lists 15 inches; neither is treated as pod spacing.

growth.short: Fine, fern-like foliage; garden plants may reach about 1–2 ft
growth.guidance: NC State and Maryland Extension describe chervil with finely divided, parsley-like leaves and a garden height up to about 2 ft; RHS gives flowering stems of 30–60 cm. These are species-level outdoor references, not a guaranteed indoor size or a named curled-leaf cultivar.

care.short: Keep the root zone evenly moist without waterlogging
care.guidance: RHS advises keeping soil or compost consistently moist but not waterlogged and watering in dry weather; containers may dry quickly in warm conditions. Light shade in hot weather and steady moisture can delay premature flowering, but no fixed indoor watering interval is established.

flowering.short: Short-lived foliage crop; small white flowers arrive relatively quickly
flowering.guidance: Maryland Extension describes delicate white flower heads and reports that chervil flowers quickly; RHS says it is usually grown as an annual although the species can be biennial. Flowering is a normal lifecycle transition and often marks declining leaf quality, not a disease symptom.

pruning.short: Remove flower stems before bloom when prioritizing leafy growth
pruning.guidance: Maryland Extension recommends cutting flower stems before bloom for denser foliage. RHS notes that once flowering begins the leaves are past their best: remove those plants for continued leaf production or leave selected plants to set seed. These are different management goals, not contradictory instructions.

harvest.short: Pick a few young leaves; cut back stems only for a larger harvest
harvest.guidance: Maryland Extension advises picking leaves just before flower buds open. RHS recommends taking only a few young leaves from each plant for ongoing harvest; for a larger cut, stems may be cut back to about 5–7.5 cm and healthy plants may produce another flush. This is garden guidance, not a guaranteed indoor regrowth interval.

uses.short: NCSU notes garden companionship with radishes and lettuces
uses.guidance: NC State lists chervil as a companion plant for radishes and lettuces and notes that its flowers attract pollinators. This is a broad garden association; the source does not establish a specific cultivar pairing, hydroponic compatibility, or a guaranteed pest-control effect.

problems.short: Hot, dry weather can hasten bolting; aphids and slugs are noted
problems.guidance: RHS says hot, dry conditions can prompt premature flowering and lists aphids as a foliage concern; NC State advises watching for slugs. Maintain moisture and cooler/lightly shaded conditions where feasible, and inspect foliage. No cultivar-specific resistance or treatment prescription is claimed.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected Extension sources describe garden and container culture but do not validate recirculating hydroponics.

evidence.note: NC State lists erect and spreading forms at species scope; this does not assign a named cultivar.
NC State and Maryland give garden heights up to 2 ft; RHS describes flowering stems at 30–60 cm. Converted to centimeters; not a fixed indoor size.
NC State lists a 1–1.5 ft width; converted to centimeters as a species-level garden reference.

spacing.reason: Outdoor spacing recommendations conflict (UMD 3–4 in thinning; NC State 15 in spacing) and neither establishes indoor pod spacing.

light.reason: Partial-to-full outdoor sun is not mapped to an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Lovage
summary: A large, hardy perennial culinary herb with celery-like foliage and edible leaves and stems. Illinois Extension reports outdoor plants about 4–6 ft tall; suitability for compact growing systems is not established.

identity.guidance: Kew POWO accepts Levisticum officinale in Apiaceae and identifies it as a temperate perennial. Illinois Extension describes its celery-like foliage and culinary use; no cultivar is assigned.

cultivation.short: Perennial herb for rich, moist soil and substantial garden space
cultivation.guidance: Illinois Extension describes lovage as a hardy perennial reaching about 4–6 feet and preferring fairly rich, moist soil; light shade may improve quality. These are garden conditions, not an indoor light tier, nutrient recipe, or proof of hydroponic compatibility.

growth.short: Large vigorous herb with dark-green, celery-like leaves
growth.guidance: Illinois Extension describes a large, vigorous perennial with leaves resembling celery and a stronger, sweeter celery-like flavor. The 4–6 ft height is retained as an outdoor species-level measurement; no compact cultivar or indoor mature size is implied.

care.short: Light shade may improve quality; keep garden soil moist
care.guidance: Illinois Extension says lovage prefers fairly rich, moist soil and that light shade improves its quality. It does not provide an indoor watering schedule or hydroponic reservoir guidance.

flowering.short: Flat-topped yellow flower heads appear in summer
flowering.guidance: Illinois Extension reports large, flat-topped yellow flower heads in summer. This is a normal seasonal feature of the species-level perennial; the source does not specify bloom timing for indoor systems or a cultivar.

harvest.short: Use young leaves and stems fresh; seed heads and roots have separate harvest cues
harvest.guidance: Illinois Extension says leaves and stems may be harvested fresh as needed, with younger leaves more tender. It advises collecting seed heads as they begin to brown, drying them in paper bags before separating the seeds, and digging roots for cool storage. No fixed harvest calendar or storage duration is stated.

uses.short: Leaves and stems season soups, salads, gravies and meat dishes
uses.guidance: Illinois Extension describes the leaves and stems as celery-like but stronger and sweeter, used in soups, salads, gravy, meat and chicken dishes; leaves are also used in teas. Stems may be candied or blanched as a vegetable. These are culinary uses, not medicinal guidance.

problems.short: Plan for a vigorous perennial rather than a compact herb
problems.guidance: The selected Illinois Extension source emphasizes lovage's large, vigorous 4–6 ft garden growth. Account for that space need outdoors; it is not evidence that the plant will fit or perform in a compact Garden system. No unsupported pest, disease, toxicity, or resistance claims are added.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected sources document outdoor garden growing, not a recirculating home hydroponic method.

growthHabits.reason: Upright perennial growth is described but a controlled habit label is not selected.

evidence.note: Illinois Extension reports 4–6 feet; outdoor regional guidance, not a cultivar-specific indoor size.

spread.reason: No mature spread is provided by the selected source.

spacing.reason: Garden placement recommendations do not establish indoor pod spacing.

light.reason: Light shade preference is not translated into an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Globe Artichoke
variety: Globe-artichoke cultivated form; no named cultivar assigned. Kew treats Cynara scolymus as a synonym within the Cynara cardunculus complex.
summary: A large thistle crop grown for its immature flower heads. Globe artichoke can be perennial in suitable warm regions or grown as an annual in colder climates; cultivar and regional chilling conditions affect bud production.

identity.short: Globe artichoke within accepted Cynara cardunculus
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Cynara cardunculus and treats Cynara scolymus as a synonym under its current classification. University of Maine Extension uses globe-artichoke crop guidance and notes cultivar differences in chilling needs; this record does not name a cultivar.

cultivation.short: A cultivar-dependent chill period can trigger reliable bud production
cultivation.guidance: University of Maine Extension reports that most artichoke varieties need about 500 hours at 35–50°F for reliable bud production, while chilling requirements differ by variety. This explains why cool exposure matters, but the Maine timing and treatment are not a universal calendar for an unnamed cultivar. Maine grows the crop as an annual because it is not reliably winter-hardy there; warmer regions may grow it as a perennial.

growth.short: Large perennial rosette sends up stalks with several sizes of edible buds
growth.guidance: The compressed-stem rosette develops one or more flowering stalks. Maine Extension describes a terminal bud, smaller secondary buds and still smaller tertiary buds; its Maine plots may carry 10–20 buds, most smaller than grocery-size heads. These counts are regional observations, not a yield promise for this unnamed cultivated form.

care.short: Keep the root zone evenly moist and give the mature plant generous garden space
care.guidance: Maine Extension recommends well-drained soil, evenly moist conditions and 1–2 inches of water per week in its field guidance; the plant does not tolerate drought well. Its Maine layout uses 2 feet between plants and at least 4 feet between rows, which is soil-bed spacing only—not hydroponic pod spacing. Base fertility on a soil test; mulch can conserve moisture and suppress weeds.

harvest.short: Cut firm buds before the bracts begin to open
harvest.guidance: Harvest while buds are firm and bracts remain closed; softening and loosening bracts indicate maturation and lower eating quality. Maine Extension's regional harvest typically starts in late July or early August and continues to hard frost, but no universal date applies. Cut with sharp clippers, leaving 2–3 inches of stem; an angled cut may reduce water pooling. Gloves help protect against spines and sticky sap. Maine Extension reports refrigerated storage for 2–3 weeks and warns that temperatures below 32°F can brown bracts; these are its regional postharvest notes, not a guaranteed shelf life.

problems.short: Watch for gray mold in cool, wet conditions and heat-related loss of vernalization
problems.guidance: Maine Extension reports gray mold as a significant disease in its trials; cool, wet or humid weather and wounds can favor infection. Water-soaked leaf or bract tissue may turn brown or black, sometimes with gray mold. Sanitation, airflow and careful harvest cuts help reduce risk. The same regional guide reports aphids and thrips and warns that high temperatures during its young-plant chilling workflow can reverse vernalization. These are documented risks, not a claim that every plant will be affected.

flowering.short: The edible artichoke is an immature flower head
flowering.guidance: The compressed-stem rosette sends up flowering stalks with a terminal bud and smaller secondary and tertiary buds. Botanically, each apparent head contains many florets. If a bud is left to mature and open, it is no longer the firm immature vegetable harvested for eating; closed, firm bracts are the useful harvest stage.

uses.guidance: The immature flower head is the edible crop; the large foliage also has ornamental value and can serve as a garden focal point where there is room to reach the plant for harvest. Maine Extension notes that secondary and small tertiary buds remain useful, including for freezing or canning, but does not provide a preservation-safety process here.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected Extension sources describe garden-field production, not a home recirculating hydroponic system.

growthHabits.reason: A large rosette habit is described but the current controlled vocabulary does not represent it without ambiguity.

evidence.note: Maine Extension reports 4–5 feet for annual production in its regional guidance; not cultivar-specific.
Maine Extension reports annual plants can exceed 3 feet in diameter; regional field context, not a cultivar-specific maximum.

spacing.reason: Outdoor crop spacing is not hydroponic pod spacing.

light.reason: The selected sources do not establish a normalized outdoor exposure class or indoor light tier.
